abstract: Eukaryotic 45S ribosomal RNA genes produce internal transcribed spacers (ITSs) that are excised and discarded during ribosome biogenesis, with no established function beyond rRNA processing. Here, we uncover an unexpected antiviral role for these seemingly expendable sequences. Comparative genomic analyses reveal extensive, evolutionarily widespread sequence similarities between eukaryotic ITSs and DNA viruses, particularly between vertebrate ITSs and herpesviruses. Across herpesvirus infections, ITS transcripts undergo striking, virus-specific remodeling, largely uncoupled from mature ribosomal RNA production. During herpes simplex virus 1 (HSV-1) infection, hierarchical Bayesian comparison of competing dynamical models favors active host ITS deployment over passive viral remodeling by odds of 174,000:1. Experimental depletion of ITS2 consistently increases infectious HSV-1 production by approximately 70%, whereas supplementation with synthetic ITS2 RNA generally suppresses viral replication. These findings reveal a previously unrecognized antiviral activity within the 45S rRNA system, challenging the view of ITSs as disposable byproducts of ribosome biogenesis.
